blocks.label: Name resolution: From a name to the next question
blocks.text: DNS is a distributed system that maps names people use to IP addresses and other DNS information. Clients usually query a resolver for a name and, when needed, consult authoritative servers.

blocks.label: Name resolution: From a name to the next question
blocks.text: Authoritative DNS is the source of information that manages a zone’s records. When name resolution fails, check the queried name, delegation, NS records, and authoritative records in order.

blocks.label: Name resolution: From a name to the next question
blocks.text: Even when DNS returns an IP address, that does not necessarily mean the web application is working properly. Name resolution comes before the connection; next, check the IP route, port, TLS, and HTTP.

blocks.text: app.example.com cannot be resolved.

blocks.label: Step 2

blocks.label: Step 3

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can separate name management issues from web application issues.

blocks.label: Records: What They Map
blocks.text: An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address, and an AAAA record maps a name to an IPv6 address. Clients use them to obtain an IP destination.

blocks.label: A CNAME record treats a name as an alias for another name. The IP address of the final destination is obtained by resolving the alias target’s name. A CNAME itself does not directly contain an IP address.
blocks.text: An NS record identifies the name servers that handle a zone. Distinguish A/AAAA, which direct IP traffic to a web service; CNAME, which creates an alias for a name; and NS, which identifies the delegation target.

blocks.label: TTL: How long cached information is used
blocks.text: TTL is the number of seconds a DNS resolver caches a record and can use it without making another query. Even after you change a record, users with a cached copy may not see the new value immediately.

blocks.label: A short TTL can help changes take effect sooner, but it increases the number of queries. A long TTL makes cached responses easier to use, but it lengthens the wait for changes to take effect.
blocks.text: If you plan to change an IP address, lower the TTL in advance rather than immediately before the change, and account for the old TTL’s expiration. After the change, verify the expected values on both the authoritative side and the resolver side before restoring the TTL.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Check the current TTL and how much time is available before the change.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Lower the TTL in advance and wait for the old TTL to expire.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: After changing the IP address, check the name resolution results and reset the TTL once they have stabilized.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: By accounting for how long the cache remains, you are less likely to mistake propagation delays for an outage.

blocks.label: DNS Is the Entry Point: HTTP and TLS Have Separate Responsibilities
blocks.text: DNS resolves names to information such as IP addresses. TCP connections, TLS certificate validation, and HTTP responses come after DNS and can each fail for different reasons.

blocks.label: If name resolution fails, checking HTTP 404s or application logs first will not get you to the cause. Conversely, even if DNS is working correctly, an HTTPS connection cannot be established if port 443 is closed.
blocks.text: During an investigation, treat name-resolution responses, IP/port connectivity, TLS, and HTTP responses as separate observations. Make changes only at the stage causing the issue; do not mask a DNS problem with broad network permissions.
